questions.q: What single dependency do model extraction, model inversion, and membership inference attacks all share?
options: They all require the attacker to have insider access to the training pipeline
They all require physical access to the server hosting the model
They all require the model to be open source
They all require a large volume of queries against the model's API to succeed
questions.explain: None of these attacks work in a handful of requests — extraction needs thousands of queries, inversion needs repeated optimization queries, and shadow-model membership inference needs enough queries to train a reliable classifier.

questions.q: What is progressive throttling, as a rate-limiting strategy?
options: Slowing response times as a caller approaches their quota, rather than cutting them off with a hard cliff
Banning every account permanently after a single query
Giving every caller unlimited queries regardless of volume
Only applying rate limits to free-tier accounts, never paid ones
questions.explain: Progressive throttling degrades attacker economics gradually while still giving legitimate bursty traffic some headroom, instead of an abrupt hard cutoff.

questions.q: Which of the following is a hallmark of an anomalous, extraction-style query pattern in API logs?
options: Near-duplicate queries that vary one feature at a time, or traffic disproportionately clustered near the decision boundary
A single query followed by no further activity from that account
Traffic evenly distributed across all hours with no feature-level pattern at all
Queries that always return the exact same label with no variation whatsoever
questions.explain: Systematic one-feature-at-a-time probing and traffic clustered near the decision boundary (where confidence is near 50/50) are shapes real, naturally varied user traffic rarely produces — they're signatures of boundary-mapping behavior.

questions.q: What does output minimization do to defend against extraction and inversion?
options: It blocks all API access entirely, which also blocks legitimate users
It controls how much each individual query is worth to an attacker, e.g. returning only a top label instead of a full confidence vector
It has no effect on either attack and is purely a performance optimization
It only works against membership inference, not extraction or inversion
questions.explain: Rate limiting controls how many queries a caller can make; output minimization controls how much each query is worth, by reducing the confidence information (the biggest accelerant for both extraction and inversion) returned per query.

questions.q: How does this chapter's defense content connect to Course 10's API security material?
options: It doesn't connect — model API defense is a completely separate discipline from general API security
Rate limiting and query monitoring here are the same API-gateway and anomaly-detection discipline from Course 10, applied to a model's prediction endpoint as the protected asset
Course 10 only covers authentication, which has nothing to do with rate limiting
API security principles apply only to REST APIs, not to model prediction endpoints
questions.explain: The rate-limiting, API-gateway, and query-monitoring practices are the same API security discipline covered in Course 10 — the new insight is recognizing a model's prediction endpoint as an asset worth protecting with it, since it guards the model's entire decision boundary.
